bp: Online shopping used to be designed around a person looking at a page, noticing product order, reading prices and reviews, and deciding what to buy. This paper asks what changes when that chooser is an autonomous AI agent acting for the shopper. The practical system is not just a recommender inside a store; it is a buyer-side agent that can read webpages or use platform interfaces, compare listings, and transact. That makes its behavior commercially important. If many shoppers delegate buying, then sellers will compete for the agent's attention rather than only the human's eye. Platforms will also need to know whether their page layout, sponsored labels, endorsements, ratings, and review counts steer agents in predictable or unfair ways. The paper builds ACES to study that question before real agentic commerce becomes too large to inspect cleanly.
wh: The hard part is that an AI agent's purchase is the end of many hidden judgments. A product may be chosen because it is cheaper, because it has better ratings, because it appears first, because it has an endorsement, or because a particular model reads a page in a particular order. In a live marketplace these factors are tangled together: popular products often have more reviews, higher placement, more endorsements, and different prices. It is also unsafe to assume that all agents share one notion of the best position on a page. The abstract says all models favored the top row, yet different models preferred different columns, which means a supposedly neutral layout may advantage products differently depending on the agent model. The central tension is measurement versus entanglement: to understand agent buying, the researchers need to separate layout effects, listing attributes, and model-specific habits.
naive: A smart beginner would send several AI agents to a real shopping site, record what they buy, and compare the final choices. That would show differences, but it would not explain them. If one model buys a higher-priced item, was it responding to ratings, review volume, position, endorsement text, or a sponsored label? Another beginner would inspect a single model and generalize from it. The abstract shows why that fails: modal choices can differ across models, and sensitivity to position, price, ratings, and reviews varies sharply. A third naive approach is to treat the top rank as a universal advantage. The paper finds that top-row bias is shared, but column preference is not universal.
ap: The core idea is to replace the messy real marketplace with a fully programmable mock marketplace where the researchers can move one piece at a time. ACES pairs a platform-agnostic agent with a sandbox store. Platform-agnostic means the agent is not built only for one merchant's website; it can interact through webpages or interfaces in a more general way. The researchers first observe aggregate choices: which products each model tends to pick when facing the same marketplace. Then they run randomized experiments. Randomized means product positions and listing attributes are deliberately varied so that a change in choice can be tied to the changed feature rather than to some unrelated product difference. This turns agentic e-commerce from anecdote into controlled measurement: what agents buy, how concentrated their choices become, and which layout or listing signals steer each model.
mech: The mechanism starts with a mock marketplace whose products and presentation can be programmed. The input is a set of product listings with visible attributes such as position on the page, price, ratings, review counts, endorsements, and sponsored tags. An AI agent is then asked to act for a consumer in that marketplace. It may parse the webpage or interact through an interface, evaluate the listings, and choose a product to buy. The first output is an aggregate choice pattern: across repeated runs or conditions, which product becomes the modal choice for each model, and whether choices concentrate on only a few products. The second stage changes from observation to experiment. The researchers randomize product positions and listing attributes, then compare how the agent's purchase changes when one signal is moved or relabeled. Position experiments ask whether row and column placement pull choices even when product substance is otherwise controlled. Attribute experiments ask whether sponsored tags reduce appeal, endorsements increase appeal, and price, ratings, and reviews affect choices in the expected direction. The key comparison is not only product A versus product B. It is also model A versus model B under the same marketplace. The output is a map of model-dependent buying behavior: shared top-row effects, different column effects, penalties for sponsored labels, rewards for endorsements, and varying sensitivity to price and review evidence.
math: The main mathematical idea is controlled comparison under uncertainty. Controlled comparison means changing one visible cause at a time, or randomizing changes so accidental product differences do not masquerade as causes. Here the uncertain thing is why the agent chose a product. A final purchase is only one observed action, but many signals could have pushed it. Randomized experiments give a cleaner language for this problem: if product position is assigned by chance, then repeated differences in buying after that assignment are evidence that position itself matters. Ranking is another core idea. A marketplace page turns many products into a visible order, and order saves attention by deciding what gets seen first. The danger is that this compression can create bias: the page location may become a reason to buy, separate from product quality. Probability appears in aggregate choices and modal choices. A modal choice is the most common outcome, useful when agents do not always make the same decision. The tradeoff is realism versus control. A sandbox may not capture all real shopping pressure, but it lets the researchers measure price, ratings, reviews, sponsored labels, endorsements, and layout separately. The paper also uses model comparison as a measurement object: the same marketplace is passed through different AI systems to expose where behavior is shared and where it depends on the model.
dots: This paper sits across three repo neighborhoods. In advertising and e-commerce, it studies how commercial attention is allocated when listings, labels, endorsements, and prices compete for a buyer's choice. In recommender systems, it reverses the usual viewpoint: instead of asking how a platform ranks products for users, it asks how an agent acting for the user ranks the platform's products. In LLM agents and tool use, it treats the model as an actor that reads, compares, and transacts, not merely as a text generator. It also connects to recurring conference ideas of ranking, probability, causal measurement, and marketplace design. The closest sibling pressure is agentic shopping evaluation, such as benchmarks for product curation and production shopping agents. ACES adds a sharper measurement question: when agents buy, which parts of the marketplace surface are steering them, and are those steering effects model-dependent enough to change competition?
ww: ACES works better than the naive real-site audit because it separates causes that real commerce naturally mixes together. If a live product is first on the page and also cheaper, a purchase tells little about whether the agent liked the price or the placement. In a programmable marketplace, the same product can be moved, tagged, endorsed, or repriced under controlled conditions. That lets the researchers turn a vague behavioral question into many small comparisons. The approach also works because it treats model identity as part of the experiment. If every model favored the top row, that suggests a shared page-reading or attention pattern. If different models prefer different columns, that shows the effect is not a universal property of e-commerce layout. Penalizing sponsored tags and rewarding endorsements are interpretable because the labels are visible listing attributes, not hidden product traits. The method should reveal practical failure modes early: seller strategies that exploit agent habits, platform layouts that unintentionally favor certain products, and regulatory issues around concentration if agents repeatedly choose only a few listings.
po: The payoff is a measurement system and an initial behavioral map for agentic e-commerce. ACES gives researchers, platforms, sellers, and regulators a way to ask what AI agents buy and why under controlled marketplace changes. The reported findings are concrete: modal choices differ across models, agents can concentrate on a few products, all models favor the top row, column effects vary by model, sponsored tags are penalized, endorsements are rewarded, and sensitivity to price, ratings, and reviews differs sharply. That buys earlier visibility into competition and platform-design risks before autonomous shopping agents become routine commercial intermediaries.
limits: The claims depend on the ACES sandbox and the models tested. A programmable mock marketplace gives control, but it may omit real-world frictions such as user budgets, brand loyalty, shipping, returns, fraud, inventory changes, and strategic seller adaptation. The abstract does not say which models were tested, how many shopping tasks were run, or whether actual consumers would approve the agents' purchases. It reports current drivers of choices, but agent behavior may change as models, prompts, tools, and marketplace interfaces change. The results show steering and model dependence; they do not prove consumer harm, illegal discrimination, or long-run market concentration by themselves.
